RGMem: Renormalization Group-based Memory Evolution for Language Agent User Profile

DOI: XXXXXXX.XXXXXXXConference: Make sure to enter the correct conference title from your rights confirmation email; June 03–05, 2018; Woodstock, NYISBN: 978-1-4503-XXXX-X/2018/06CCS: User modeling, personalization and recommendation
Ao Tian Note: Both authors contributed equally to this research. email: tianao@buaa.edu.cn Affiliation: Beihang University, China , Yunfeng Lu email: lyf@buaa.edu.cn Affiliation: Beihang University, China , Xinxin Fan email: fanxinxin@ict.ac.cn Affiliation: Institute of Computing Technology, Chinese Academy of Science, China , Changhao Wang email: wch@buaa.edu.cn Affiliation: Beihang University, China , Lanzhi Zhou email: piki@buaa.edu.cn Affiliation: Beihang University, China , Yeyao Zhang email: zhangyeyao@guangfan.ai Affiliation: LightSail, China and Yanfang Liu email: hannahlyf@buaa.edu.cn Affiliation: Beihang University, China
Received  5 June 2009
Abstract.

Personalized and continuous interactions are the key to enhancing user experience in today’s large language model (LLM)-based conversational systems, however, the finite context windows and static parametric memory make it difficult to model the cross-session long-term user states and behavioral consistency. Currently, the existing solutions to this predicament, such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and explicit memory systems, primarily focus on fact-level storage and retrieval, lacking the capability to distill latent preferences and deep traits from the multi-turn dialogues, which limits the long-term and effective user modeling, directly leading to the personalized interactions remaining shallow, and hindering the cross-session continuity. To realize the long-term memory and behavioral consistency for Language Agents in LLM era, we propose a self-evolving memory framework RGMem, inspired by the ideology of classic renormalization group (RG) in physics, this framework enables to organize the dialogue history in multiple scales: it first extracts semantics and user insights from episodic fragments, then through hierarchical coarse-graining and rescaling operations, progressively forms a dynamically-evolved user profile. The core innovation of our work lies in modeling memory evolution as a multi-scale process of information compression and emergence, which accomplishes the high-level and accurate user profiles from noisy and microscopic-level interactions. As a result, a multi-granularity retrieval mechanism is gained to achieve coordination on both detailed and abstract memories, by which the Language Agent’s cross-session continuity and personalized interactive capability can be remarkably boosted. Finally, multi-facet experiments on the Long-term Conversational Memory (LOCOMO) Benchmark demonstrate that our proposed RGMem establishes a new state-of-the-art, outperforming the strongest baseline method by over 7 absolute percentage points in overall accuracy.

Keywords: 
Memory Framework, User Profile Modeling, Personalization, Language Agent, Conversational Systems, Knowledge Graph

1. Introduction

User profiling in recommender systems is centered in population-level interactions, that is, uses’ features are usually embedded into latent space and clustered to optimize retrieval and ranking (Zhao et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2018; Middleton et al., 2004; Lu et al., 2016; Fkih, 2022). In contrast, the personal dialog-based assistant continuously ingests fine-grained, first-hand signals from a single user across her/his activity, diet, social life, daily work, and emotions, with context and preferences evolving over time. Naively transplanting group-level embedding/clustering into dialog-based user profiling would sacrifice individual distinction, break evidence traceability, and lead to imbalanced choices of abstraction levels.

To tackle the predicament above, we think the core challenge lies in the dialog continuity, i.e., anchoring a set of trait-level invariants across dialog sessions while rapidly adapting to new evidence. As well known, the currently-existing memory and retrieval mechanisms struggle to achieve this balance. Limited context windows and the "lost-in-the-middle (Liu et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2024)" effect make long-dialog unreliable, implying the static parametric (implicit) memory is difficult to update incrementally (Wang and Chen, 2025). Although retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) (Edge et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2024) and explicit memory systems attempt to solve this problem at the fact level, they bring lexical overlap and recency, making it hard to abstract stable, higher-level traits across dialog sessions, thus giving rise to accumulation of conflict and ignorance of low-frequency but semantically consistent weak signals. More importantly, the dialog personalization is inherently multi-scale, that is to say, it must precisely localize the concrete events (micro), compose cross-situational relations and regularities (meso), and ultimately distill long-term, stable, and updatable profile invariants (macro). This raises the classic stability-plasticity dilemma: how to preserve slow variables (long-term traits) while rapidly migrating the profile’s center of mass when genuine changes occur.

We think the essence of dialog-based user profiling is not merely a retrieval problem but a cross-scale evolution problem, regarding this point, it can be naturally aligned with the classic renormalization group (RG) (Parisen Toldin, 2022; Ma, 1973; Tu, 2023) concept in physics, that is, RG enables to iteratively coarse-grain and rescale to retain modes that remain relevant across different scales, attenuate irrelevant noise, and converge along flows to stable fixed-point descriptions. In other words, when evidence crosses thresholds, phase transition occurs and the system enters a new state. Mapped to the dialog-memory problem in this paper: noisy turn-level details are coarse-grained into scenario facts and user conclusions (micro → meso), further integrated into behavioral regularities and abstract traits (meso → macro); through selective integration and thresholding triggers, predictive trait invariants stabilize, and the profile’s center of mass migrates when major preference shift arises.

Inspired by the ideology of renormalization group in physics, we propose an explicit self-evolving memory framework RGMem. The RG principles of cross-scale coarse-grained and invariant preservation are engineered into layered-memory organization with principled updates and propagation (Tu, 2023; Zhu et al., 2022; Ma, 1973; Liu and Yu, 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a; Rezazadeh et al., 2024), enabling stable emergence from facts to traits and rapid migration under real preference changes. Our proposed RGMem upgrades "store-and-retrieve" to "understand-and-evolve", delivering auditable and evolved personalization without modifying model parameters. In our work, we treat RG as an engineering principle for multi-scale organization and evolution, rather than physical modeling per se. In a nutshell, three main contributions are involved:

  • •

    We propose a principled multi-scale self-evolving memory framework to unify scenario memory, dynamic relation graphs, and hierarchical summaries, providing multi-granularity retrievals to match queries at different abstraction levels.

  • •

    We introduce three types of explicit evolution operators that enable change-aware updates, weighted selection, and hierarchical propagation, with purpose of balancing evidence traceability with the stability-plasticity trade-off.

  • •

    Muti-facet experiments on LOCOMO datasets are conducted to validate the effectiveness of our work, and the experimental results showcase our proposed RGMem significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art baseline methods.

2. Related Work

2.1. User Modeling in Recommender Systems

User modeling in recommender systems typically relies on large-scale user–item interactions to learn population-level latent representations for retrieval and ranking (Zhao et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2018; Lu et al., 2016; Fkih, 2022). Representative approaches include collaborative filtering and matrix factorization, graph-based recommendation, and deep representation/embedding models. More recently, multi-interest representation-learning models have been explored to improve diversity of expression. However, these methods target structured interaction signals and population-level statistical objectives, making them ill-suited to cover the high-dimensional textual signals present in open-domain dialogs, such as events, facts, and pragmatic preferences, etc. Moreover, they also lack interpretable, traceable evidence chains and mechanisms for dynamic evolution across sessions, falling short of the necessity of dialog-based personalized user profiling (Zhao et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b; Li et al., 2024).

2.2. Dialog Personalization and Implicit Memory

Implicit memory internalizes the personalized information into model parameters via supervised fine-tuning or parameter-efficient adaptation (Wang et al., 2024; Tan et al., 2025a; Wei et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2025), eliminating the need for retrieval at inference and suiting pattern-level induction of style and preferences. Yet its core shortcomings conflict with the demands of dialog personalization, that is, it requires modifying or retraining parameters, which makes it hard to directly interoperate with closed-source high-capability models, and inconvenient for sharing a unified profile across models. Although latent-space memory can manifest as parameters, external memory matrices, hidden states, soft prompts, or key–value (KV) (Gershman et al., 2025) caches, most approaches still rely on retraining to function effectively; KV cache–based methods are closer to long-context methods than to true memory systems that support abstraction, integration, and reasoning. Furthermore, implicit memory offers limited auditability, fine-grained incremental updates, and rollback capability, making it hard to robustly carry factual details and long-term evolution. Overall, implicit memory does not match dialog personalization’s core requirement of "traceable user-profiling with continual evolution".

2.3. Explicit Memory and RAG

Explicit memory externalizes user-related information for persistent storage and retrieves it during generation (Rasmussen et al., 2025; Chhikara et al., 2025). This line of work offers advantages in traceability, persistence, and online updates. Nevertheless, existing systems often focus on "better retrieval" and explicit fact logging. The aggregation/summarization mechanisms are geared toward paragraph- or card-level storage and lack capabilities for understanding and mining memory, which makes it difficult to distill implicit preferences, habits, and traits from multiple situations (Pan et al., 2025; Tan et al., 2025b). As a result, they are prone to retrieval–generation mismatches and broken evidence chains. Contradiction and noise accumulate over time without principled management, the profile struggles to evolve stably and faithfully into a continuously updated user profiling.

3. Methodology

3.1. Preliminaries and Motivation

The Renormalization Group (RG) is a theoretical framework originating from statistical physics, aiming to understand how macroscopic phenomena emerge from microscopic details (Wilson, 1983; Pelissetto and Vicari, 2002; Litim, 2001; Zinn-Justin, 2007; Yakhot and Orszag, 1986). From the perspective of computational and information sciences, RG provides a unified principle for organizing and compressing multi-scale information. Its core idea is to systematically "integrate out" irrelevant, high-frequency details (noise) at a given scale through iterative coarse-graining operations, while preserving the relevant invariants that are decisive for the system’s long-range behavior and macroscopic state. This process causes the effective parameters describing the system to evolve along a renormalization flow and eventually converge to fixed points that describe the macroscopic essence of the system in its most concise form.

Although RG originated from physics science, its ideas for handling multi-scale complex systems have influenced several areas of machine learning. For instance, some research interprets the layer-wise abstraction process of deep neural networks as an approximate RG flow, where each layer coarse-grains the input information (Chen et al., 2018; Di Sante et al., 2022; Bény, 2013; Wang and Liu, 2025). Another works have established deep connections between the Information Bottleneck principle from information theory and RG’s principle of invariant preservation (Tishby and Zaslavsky, 2015; Mehta and Schwab, 2014). In the field of graph representation learning, hierarchical pooling and graph coarsening algorithms have also drawn inspiration from RG’s ideology to learn structured representations of graphs at different scales (Ying et al., 2018).

However, these studies primarily treat RG as an analogy or a tool for static data representation learning. To the best of our knowledge, applying RG as a complete, dynamic, and evolutionary framework for building long-term memory in language agents remains an unexplored area. The construction of conversational user profiles, presents a core challenge that is fundamentally rooted in this multi-scale nature of information, namely the inherent stability-plasticity dilemma: a system must precisely process transient, specific microscopic interactions while enabling the emergence of long-term, stable macroscopic patterns. From the perspective of theoretical modeling, this challenge can be formalized as a variational problem to find an optimal user-profiling theory 𝒯∗\mathcal{T}^{*}.

To explore this issue, we define an effective Hamiltonian function of user persona, ℋ⁡(𝒯)\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{T}), as a cost function that measures the quality of any given use-profiling theory 𝒯\mathcal{T}. An ideal use profiling theory should minimize the "energy" of this Hamiltonian function. Conceptually, it consists of three terms to reflect "energy":

(1) ℋ⁡(𝒯)=α​Ec​o​n​s​i​s​t​e​n​c​y​(𝒯)+β​Ef​i​d​e​l​i​t​y​(𝒯|𝒟L​0)+γ​Ec​o​m​p​l​e​x​i​t​y​(𝒯),\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{T})=\alpha E_{consistency}(\mathcal{T})+\beta E_{fidelity}(\mathcal{T}|\mathcal{D}_{L0})+\gamma E_{complexity}(\mathcal{T}),

where Ec​o​n​s​i​s​t​e​n​c​yE_{consistency} is used to penalize the internal contradictions within the theory, Ef​i​d​e​l​i​t​yE_{fidelity} penalizes deviations from the microscopic evidence 𝒟L​0\mathcal{D}_{L0}, and Ec​o​m​p​l​e​x​i​t​yE_{complexity} penalizes the overfitting and redundancy. The goal of our approach is to find the ground state solution of this Hamiltonian, i.e., the optimal use-profiling theory

(2) 𝒯∗=arg⁡min𝒯⁡ℋ⁡(𝒯).\displaystyle\mathcal{T}^{*}=\arg\min_{\mathcal{T}}\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{T}).

As well known, directly solving this Hamiltonian function, defined over a high-dimensional, heterogeneous-text space, is intractable. Towards this end, we introduce the Renormalization Group ideology–a fundamental theory from physics to solve such multi-scale system problems–as the first principles for our solution design. Accordingly, our proposed RGMem is naturally designed as a heuristic variational minimization algorithm for ℋ⁡(𝒯)\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{T}) at multiple scales, with its architecture being a direct computational instantiation of the three core RG principles:

  • •

    Initial Coarse-Graining: To define Hamiltonian function on a computable discrete space, our initial module realizes RG’s requirement of discretizing and coarse-graining a high-noise continuous field by transforming the continuous input stream into a set of discrete microscopic states.

  • •

    Parameter Flow: To iteratively lower the energy at different scales, a structured theoretical space and a series of transformation operators embody the RG dynamics of coupling parameters flowing under scale transformations. Each step of transformation aims to find a lower-energy theory that properly describes the system’s ground state as a combination of a dominant macroscopic order (the order parameter) and unavoidable intrinsic conflicts (the correction terms).

  • •

    Dynamic Convergence: To find the stable attractor basins of the global optimum, the framework’s intrinsic dynamical mechanisms are designed to capture the long-term behavior of RG flow, enabling it to naturally derive the stable convergence of the theory (corresponding to fixed points at energy minima) and non-linear transitions under specific conditions (corresponding to phase transitions from one energy minimum to another).

Based on these three principles, we construct the following formal model and its algorithmic instantiation.

3.2. Use-Profiling Modeling

Inspired by the renormalization group principles, we formalize our RGMem as a mathematical system composed of three core objects: memory state space, multi-scale effective theory defined on user profiling, and renormalization group transformations driving from the evolution of user-profiling theory.

Memory State Space: The complete memory state of a system is defined within a unified state space ℳ\mathcal{M}, and formulated as the Cartesian product of the microscopic evidence space 𝒟L​0\mathcal{D}_{L0} and the structured knowledge space 𝒢\mathcal{G}:

(3) ℳ=𝒟L​0×𝒢\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{D}_{L0}\times\mathcal{G}

where 𝒟L​0={d1,d2,…}\mathcal{D}_{L0}=\{d_{1},d_{2},...\} is a set of discrete episodic memory units (Fountas et al., 2025; Pan et al., 2025; Nan et al., 2025), representing the system’s microscopic foundation, and 𝒢=(𝒱,ℰ)\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}) denotes a dynamic knowledge graph with a specific hierarchical structure (Niu et al., 2025), wherein 𝒱\mathcal{V} is the set of vertices and ℰ\mathcal{E} is the set of edges, providing a structured basis for information organization and knowledge evolution.

Multi-Scale Effective Theory: We define an Effective Theory 𝒯⁡(ℳ,s)\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{M},s) as an effective parameterized description of the user profile information contained within the memory state ℳ\mathcal{M} at a specific observation scale ss. This theory is defined by a set of relevant effective coupling parameters {λi​(s)}\{\lambda_{i}(s)\} at that scale. Different scales correspond to different levels of abstraction, from microscopic evidence at s=0s=0 to mesoscopic and macroscopic patterns at s≥1s\geq 1.

Renormalization Group Transformation: The RG Transformation ℛ\mathcal{R} is the core operator that drives the evolution of effective theory across different scales, aiming to progressively find low-energy solutions to Hamiltonian ℋ⁡(𝒯)\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{T}), by which it can map an effective theory 𝒯(s)\mathcal{T}^{(s)} at scale ss to a new and more coarse-grained effective theory 𝒯(s+1)\mathcal{T}^{(s+1)} at scale s+1s+1. This process is described by a discrete RG Flow equation:

(4) 𝒯(s+1)=ℛ⁡(𝒯(s)).\mathcal{T}^{(s+1)}=\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{T}^{(s)}).

This RG transformation operator conceptually involves two steps: coarse-graining and rescaling.

3.3. Renormalization Flow: Operators and Instantiation

The RGMem algorithm instantiates the abstract formal model defined in Section 3.1 through a three-layer architecture (L0, L1, and L2). The L0 layer (microscopic layer) is responsible for constructing the microscopic evidence space 𝒟L​0\mathcal{D}_{L0}; the L1 layer (mesoscopic evolution layer) constructs the knowledge space 𝒢\mathcal{G} as a mesoscopic structure and instantiates the renormalization transformation operators ℛ\mathcal{R} that drive the evolution of effective theories from mesoscopic to macroscopic scales; and the L2 layer (observation layer) implements the multi-scale observation function fr​e​t​rf_{retr}. The following subsections will detail their implementation mechanisms.

3.3.1. Construction of Memory State Space

The proposed RGMem instantiates the memory state space through the initial processing pipelines of its L0 and L1 layers.

Construction of Microscopic Evidence Space 𝒟L​0\mathcal{D}_{L0}: The space 𝒟L​0\mathcal{D}_{L0} is generated from the raw dialogue stream Dr​a​wD_{raw} by a two-stage initial coarse-grained function fc​g=fs​y​n​t​h∘fs​e​gf_{cg}=f_{synth}\circ f_{seg}. First, the segmentation function fs​e​gf_{seg} discretizes Dr​a​wD_{raw} into a series of episodic units. Second, the synthesis function fs​y​n​t​hf_{synth} maps each episodic unit to a structured microscopic state d∈𝒟L​0d\in\mathcal{D}_{L0}. Each state dd is defined as a tuple containing the parameters for its initial theory:

(5) d=(λf​a​c​t,Λc​o​n​c),d=(\lambda_{fact},\Lambda_{conc}),

where λf​a​c​t\lambda_{fact} is the objective configuration parameter (core fact), and Λc​o​n​c\Lambda_{conc} is a user conclusion parameter set pre-separated by relevance, it is a union of two disjoint subsets: Λc​o​n​c=Λb​a​s​e∪Λr​e​l\Lambda_{conc}=\Lambda_{base}\cup\Lambda_{rel}, where Λb​a​s​e\Lambda_{base} contains objective, user-centric event parameters derived from λf​a​c​t\lambda_{fact}, and Λr​e​l\Lambda_{rel} is the high-relevant conclusion subset considered as the "seed" for future macroscopic order parameters.

Structured Knowledge Space 𝒢\mathcal{G}: The initial construction of 𝒢\mathcal{G} is accomplished by a hierarchical extraction function fe​x​t​r​a​c​tf_{extract} that acts on the generated microscopic evidence space 𝒟L​0\mathcal{D}_{L0}:

(6) fe​x​t​r​a​c​t:𝒟L​0→𝒢.f_{extract}:\mathcal{D}_{L0}\rightarrow\mathcal{G}.

This function instantiates a multi-scale "lattice" structure 𝒱=𝒱a​b​s∪𝒱g​e​n∪𝒱i​n​s​t\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{V}_{abs}\cup\mathcal{V}_{gen}\cup\mathcal{V}_{inst}, where 𝒱a​b​s\mathcal{V}_{abs} (Abstract Concepts) is the set of top-level taxonomic concepts corresponding to the system’s slow-varying degrees of freedom, 𝒱g​e​n\mathcal{V}_{gen} (General Events) denotes the set of standardized activities, and 𝒱i​n​s​t\mathcal{V}_{inst} (Instance Events) is the set of unique instances corresponding to the fast-varying degrees of freedom. Concurrently, the function establishes the connections between entities, forming the relation set ℰ\mathcal{E}. This set is explicitly partitioned into two disjoint subsets: ℰ=ℰc​l​s∪ℰe​v​t\mathcal{E}=\mathcal{E}_{cls}\cup\mathcal{E}_{evt}, where ℰc​l​s\mathcal{E}_{cls} is the set of static classification relations defining the system’s static topological backbone, and ℰe​v​t\mathcal{E}_{evt} is the set of dynamic event relations defining the system’s dynamical interactions.

3.3.2. Instantiation of Renormalization Group Operators

The evolution of effective theory 𝒯\mathcal{T} attached to the knowledge graph 𝒢\mathcal{G} is driven by three transformation operators, which together constitute the concrete solution for the multi-scale variational minimization of Hamiltonian function ℋ⁡(𝒯)\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{T}).

Relation Inference Operator ℛK​1\mathcal{R}_{K1}: This operator acts on each element ee of the dynamic event relation subset ℰe​v​t\mathcal{E}_{evt}, driving the evolution of mesoscopic theory via an incremental flow equation. Let 𝒯e(1,t)\mathcal{T}_{e}^{(1,t)} be the mesoscopic theory at time step tt, the evolution at time step t+1t+1 can be formulated as:

(7) 𝒯e(1,t+1)←𝒯e(1,t)+β⁡(𝒯e(1,t),Den​e​w),\mathcal{T}_{e}^{(1,t+1)}\leftarrow\mathcal{T}_{e}^{(1,t)}+\beta(\mathcal{T}_{e}^{(1,t)},D_{e}^{new}),

where Den​e​wD_{e}^{new} is the set of new microscopic evidence associated with relation ee. The non-linear transformation function β⁡(⋅)\beta(\cdot), implemented by an LLM, integrates the present theory with new evidence to output an updated effective theory 𝒯e(1,t+1)\mathcal{T}_{e}^{(1,t+1)}. Its effective coupling parameters {λi​(1)}\{\lambda_{i}(1)\} contain a summary and potential inference on the state of relation ee. The concrete execution of this operator is controlled by a threshold θi​n​f\theta_{inf}.

Node-Level Block Transformation Operator ℛK​2\mathcal{R}_{K2}: This operator acts on each node vv of the abstract concept subset 𝒱a​b​s\mathcal{V}_{abs}, performing a block-spin-like transformation. Its input is a mixed-scale set of new evidence ℐvn​e​w\mathcal{I}_{v}^{new} defined as:

(8) ℐvn​e​w={𝒯ei(1),n​e​w}i∈N⁡(v)∪{djn​e​w}j∈D⁡(v),\mathcal{I}_{v}^{new}=\{\mathcal{T}_{e_{i}}^{(1),new}\}_{i\in N(v)}\cup\{d_{j}^{new}\}_{j\in D(v)},

where N⁡(v)N(v) is the set of relations associated with node vv, and D⁡(v)D(v) is the set of microscopic evidence associated with those relations. {𝒯ei(1),n​e​w}\{\mathcal{T}_{e_{i}}^{(1),new}\} is the set of recently updated mesoscopic theories in N⁡(v)N(v), while {djn​e​w}\{d_{j}^{new}\} is the set of newly arrived microscopic evidence in D⁡(v)D(v). This operator is also decomposed into a composition of two sub-operations: ℛK​2=𝕊∘ℙ\mathcal{R}_{K2}=\mathbb{S}\circ\mathbb{P}, where 𝕊\mathbb{S} and ℙ\mathbb{P} respectively denotes projection-selection sub-operation and synthesis-rescaling sub-operation as follows.

The Projection-Selection Sub-Operation ℙ\mathbb{P} performs coarse-graining. It acts on the input set ℐvn​e​w\mathcal{I}_{v}^{new} and filters it using relevance principle, which prioritizes the theory parameters that have already been partially renormalized and possess higher information density over more primitive microscopic evidence, which ensures the efficiency and directionality of the coarse-graining process, making the construction of macroscopic theory predominantly guided by more relevant parameters that contain collective behavior information. Consequently, the output becomes a filtered evidence set Dv′=ℙ⁡(ℐvn​e​w)D^{\prime}_{v}=\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{I}_{v}^{new}).

The Synthesis-Rescaling Sub-Operation 𝕊\mathbb{S} performs rescaling, combining Dv′D^{\prime}_{v} with the old theory 𝒯v(2,t)\mathcal{T}_{v}^{(2,t)} to reconstruct a new multi-parameter theory 𝒯v(2,t+1)\mathcal{T}_{v}^{(2,t+1)}. This new theory consists of two distinct types of parameters:

  • •

    Order Parameter Σ(2)\Sigma^{(2)}: This parameter aims to capture the universal patterns that emerge during coarse-graining and define the system’s macroscopic state. It represents the dominant macroscopic mode that maximally reduces the system’s internal contradiction energy (Ec​o​n​s​i​s​t​e​n​c​yE_{consistency}), while balancing complexity (Ec​o​m​p​l​e​x​i​t​yE_{complexity}) and fidelity (Ef​i​d​e​l​i​t​yE_{fidelity}).

  • •

    Correction Term Δ(2)\Delta^{(2)}: This parameter aims to preserve the salient information crucial for an accurate description of the system’s state, while not universally applicable. It represents the inherent "tension" or "frustration" in the system’s ground state, which must be acknowledged to maintain fidelity to microscopic evidence (Ef​i​d​e​l​i​t​yE_{fidelity}) when the internal contradiction energy (Ec​o​n​s​i​s​t​e​n​c​yE_{consistency}) cannot be reduced to zero.

These two parameters are defined as:

(9) Σ(2,t+1)=Aggc​o​m​m​o​n​(Dv′,Σ(2,t)),\Sigma^{(2,t+1)}=\text{Agg}_{common}(D^{\prime}_{v},\Sigma^{(2,t)}),
(10) Δ(2,t+1)=Extracts​a​l​i​e​n​t​(Dv′,Δ(2,t)),\Delta^{(2,t+1)}=\text{Extract}_{salient}(D^{\prime}_{v},\Delta^{(2,t)}),

where Aggc​o​m​m​o​n\text{Agg}_{common} and Extracts​a​l​i​e​n​t\text{Extract}_{salient} are non-linear functions focused on commonality aggregation and salience extraction, respectively. Similarly, the concrete execution of this operator is controlled by a threshold θs​u​m\theta_{sum}.

Hierarchical Flow Operator ℛK​3\mathcal{R}_{K3}: This operator embodies the iterative nature of RG, driving information flow upwards along the static topological backbone ℰc​l​s\mathcal{E}_{cls}. It acts on sets of macroscopic theories at scales s≥2s\geq 2, aiming to reach a fixed-point theory. For each parent node vp∈𝒱a​b​sv_{p}\in\mathcal{V}_{abs}, the transformation is defined as:

(11) (Σvp(s+1),Δvp(s+1))=ℛK​3​({(Σvci(s),Δvci(s))}i),(\Sigma_{v_{p}}^{(s+1)},\Delta_{v_{p}}^{(s+1)})=\mathcal{R}_{K3}(\{(\Sigma_{v_{c_{i}}}^{(s)},\Delta_{v_{c_{i}}}^{(s)})\}_{i}),

where ℛK​3\mathcal{R}_{K3} operator is to perform Synergy/Tension Analysis to distill common patterns and internal conflicts. Its execution is scheduled by a dirty-flag propagation mechanism.

3.4. Dynamics and Multi-Scale Observations

3.4.1. Emergent Dynamics: Fixed Points and Phase Transitions

The long-term dynamics of RG flow, driven by RG transformation, exhibit two salient modes: convergence to a stable state and abrupt structural shifts under specific conditions. These two behaviors correspond to the concepts of Fixed Point and Phase Transition in RG theory, which can exactly guide our methodology.

Fixed Point Converges Effective Theory. A core property of the RG flow is its convergence towards specific regions in the theoretical parameter space. In our framework, a mature and stable user profiling corresponds dynamically to an Attractive Fixed Point. In theory, a fixed-point theory 𝒯∗\mathcal{T}^{*} means it remains invariant under the RG transformation, i.e., ℛ⁡(𝒯∗)=𝒯∗\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{T}^{*})=\mathcal{T}^{*}. In the practical operation for our RGMem, this means that when new microscopic evidence consistent with the user’s existing profile flows in, its impact on the macroscopic theory (i.e., the effective coupling parameters (Σ(s),Δ(s))(\Sigma^{(s)},\Delta^{(s)}) at scales s≥2s\geq 2) approaches zero: 𝒯(s,t+1)≈𝒯(s,t)\mathcal{T}^{(s,t+1)}\approx\mathcal{T}^{(s,t)}. This stability arises from the attractor nature of the fixed point. As evidence accumulates, the RG flow driven by operators ℛK​2\mathcal{R}_{K2} and ℛK​3\mathcal{R}_{K3} guides the effective theory point 𝒯(s)\mathcal{T}^{(s)} to converge towards the attractor basin of a fixed point 𝒯∗\mathcal{T}^{*}.

Phase Transition Reshapes Effective Theory. Long-term user traits are not immutable, this is understood in our framework as the system undergoing a phase transition. A phase transition refers to a qualitative change in the macroscopic properties of a system (i.e., the order parameter Σ\Sigma) as a control parameter crosses a critical point. In our RGMem, this control parameter is the cumulative strength and consistency of new evidence that is incongruous with the existing fixed-point theory 𝒯A∗\mathcal{T}^{*}_{A}. When a large volume of anomalous evidence flows in, it creates a strong "tension" in the theoretical space, attempting to pull the theory point 𝒯\mathcal{T} from the current fixed point 𝒯A∗\mathcal{T}^{*}_{A} towards another potential attractor 𝒯B∗\mathcal{T}^{*}_{B}. The aforementioned thresholds (θi​n​f,θs​u​m\theta_{inf},\theta_{sum}) act as the critical points in this process. Only when the cumulative strength of the anomalous evidence is sufficient to cross these thresholds and trigger one or more significant renormalization transformations can a global restructuring of the system occur, leading to a drastic change in the order parameter Σ\Sigma, and completing a paradigm shift in the effective user-profiling theories.

3.4.2. Multi-Scale Observations

A complete dynamical framework ought to define not only the system’s evolution but also how to observe its state. In RGMem, this function is fulfilled by the multi-scale retrieval mechanism of the L2 layer, which plays the role of observation operators in our theoretical framework.

The core of this mechanism is a multi-scale joint retrieval function fr​e​t​r​(q,ℳ)f_{retr}(q,\mathcal{M}). Upon the query qq, this function triggers parallel probes of the effective theory at different scales, with its output C⁡(q)C(q) being a multi-granularity context that synergistically integrates the observation results. The core function of fr​e​t​rf_{retr} is to extract information from different scales based on the adjustable observation scale in the query instruction.

Probing Microscopic States (s=0s=0): This acts directly on the Memory State Space ℳ\mathcal{M} to retrieve un-renormalized microscopic evidence relevant to the query qq.

Probing Mesoscopic and Macroscopic Theories (s≥1s\geq 1): This acts on the effective theory attached to the structured knowledge space 𝒢\mathcal{G}. This operation can precisely extract theories at specific levels, such as the mesoscopic relation theory 𝒯e(1)\mathcal{T}_{e}^{(1)} at scale s=1s=1, or the macroscopic node theory 𝒯v(s≥2)\mathcal{T}_{v}^{(s\geq 2)} with its order parameter (Σ\Sigma) and correction term (Δ\Delta) at scales s≥2s\geq 2.

Ultimately, the "measurement results" from different scales are aggregated and formatted into a unified context document C⁡(q)C(q). This design realizes the cross-scale consistency in our framework, ensuring that the complete evidence chain from microscopic details to macroscopic patterns can be presented coherently and synergistically, thereby effectively translating RGMem’s internal multi-scale structure into external, usable conversational capabilities.

4. Experiment Evaluation

This chapter presents a comprehensive evaluation of our proposed RGMem framework through multi-facet experiments on a long-term conversational memory benchmark. Our experiment design aims to answer the basic research questions: i) How does the overall performance of RGMem compare to the SOTA baseline methods in maintaining long-term conversational consistency (RQ1)? ii) To what extent is the performance advantage of our RGMem attributable to its core, renormalization group-inspired hierarchical evolution structure, rather than merely to high-quality fact extraction (RQ2)? and iii) How sensitive is the performance of RGMem to its core parameters? Does the framework exhibit robustness around its theory-driven, principled parameter settings (RQ3)?

4.1. Experimental Setup

We evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed RGMem framework on the challenging long-term conversational memory benchmark LOCOMO (Maharana et al., 2024). We demonstrate the superiority of our framework by comparing it against a comprehensive suite of strong baselines and conducting in-depth ablation studies on its core components.

All experiments are conducted using "gpt-4.1-mini" as the base language model. For evaluation, we report the LLM-judge score across four reasoning dimensions: Single-Hop, Multi-Hop, Temporal, and Open-Domain. Further details on the dataset, baseline descriptions, and our specific implementation parameters are provided in Appendix A.

4.2. Main Performance (Answering RQ1)

Overall Performance. As shown in Table 1, our RGMem achieves an overall average score of 86.17%, and significantly surpasses all the baselines. It demonstrates a substantial performance gain of over 7% points compared to the best baseline Zep (79.09%), and its performance closely approaches the theoretical upper bound of Full-Context (87.52%). This result empirically validates the overall superiority of our framework at a macroscopic level.

Single-Hop Reasoning: For the single-hop reasoning tasks, RGMem achieves a score of 89.58%, surpassing the theoretical upper bound of Full-Context (88.53%). This result reveals the value of our initial coarse-graining process. While Full-Context provides complete information, it also introduces significant noise, redundancy, and potential distractors, posing a challenge for the LLM to precisely locate facts within a vast amount of text. In contrast, our RGMem’s initial coarse-graining function (fc​gf_{cg}) pre-processes the noisy raw dialogues into high signal-to-noise ratio core facts (λf​a​c​t\lambda_{fact}) and user conclusions (Λc​o​n​c\Lambda_{conc}), which implies the distilled and condensed information to the LLM for single-hop queries is more effective than the complete but noisy raw context, thereby achieving exceptionally high fact retrieval accuracy.

Multi-Hop Reasoning. For this category of reasoning tasks, our RGMem exhibits the most significant performance gain, achieving a score of 78.03% and outperforming the best baseline Zep (69.16%), by nearly 9%. This advantage stems from our framework’s complete hierarchical evolution capability. The intrinsic challenge of multi-hop reasoning is that the required evidence is often dispersed across multiple non-contiguous parts of the dialogue history. While the traditional RAG methods can only retrieve these isolated facts at query time, leaving the entire burden of integration to the LLM, our RGMem’s relation inference operator (ℛK​1\mathcal{R}_{K1}) and Node-level Block Transformation Operator (ℛK​2\mathcal{R}_{K2}) can identify and consolidate the latent connections between these discrete facts in advance during the memory evolution process, forming coherent, thematic summaries. For complex queries that require reasoning across different thematic domains, the Hierarchical Flow Operator (ℛK​3\mathcal{R}_{K3}) plays a crucial role. This operator iterates upwards along the static topological skeleton, performing "Synergy/Tension Analysis" on summaries from different child nodes to form a global, more macroscopic user profiling. Consequently, RGMem can provide a context that has been integrated from local to global scales across multiple hierarchical levels, thereby it effectively address the predicament of multi-hop reasoning.

Temporal Reasoning. RGMem’s leading performance (88.91%) on temporal tasks validates the effectiveness of our framework’s dynamic evolution mechanism. Through its threshold-based dynamic evolution operators (ℛK​1,ℛK​2\mathcal{R}_{K1},\mathcal{R}_{K2}), our RGMem can distinguish between incidental noise and persistent trends, performing non-linear, structural reshaping of the use profile when a user preference undergoes a phase transition, thus accurately capturing the user’s dynamic changes.

Open-Domain Reasoning. The performance margin of our RGMem in open-domain tasks is relatively smaller. This is consistent with our framework’s design principles. These types of questions are typically broader and less related to the user’s core and stable traits. Our RGMem’s coarse-graining process is designed to preserve the user’s relevant invariants across scales while intentionally filtering out what is deemed as high-entropy, non-core irrelevant information. While this principled information filtering mechanism may limit its performance in this specific dimension, it is precisely what ensures RGMem can rely on a stable, high signal-to-noise ratio core user profile for reasoning in the more critical multi-hop and temporal tasks.

Summary. These multi-dimensional experimental results demonstrate that the good performance of RGMem is not coincidental. Its performance across each dimension deeply reflects the unique working mechanisms of RG-inspired framework. Through hierarchical evolution and principled information filtering, our proposed RGMem can successfully address the stability-plasticity dilemma in user-profile modeling.

4.3. Ablation Study (Answering RQ2)

The results of the ablation study in Table 2 quantify the contribution of each core component in our multi-scale framework, and reveal their powerful synergistic effect. The variant model w/o L0, which utilizes only the evolved artifacts from L1 and higher levels, exhibits a drastic drop in performance, which unveils that higher-level theories must be grounded in the microscopic evidence (𝒟L​0\mathcal{D}_{L0}) of the L0 layer. Conversely, the performance gap of the variant model w/o L1 using only microscopic evidence, particularly its significant deficiency in the multi-hop and temporal reasoning tasks which are the most demanding in terms of structure and dynamic evolution, proves that the scattered evidence requires the higher-level structured knowledge (𝒢\mathcal{G}) for effective guidance. Therefore, the superior performance of the full RGMem framework is attributed to the ability to provide a context that synergistically combines macroscopic theories with microscopic evidence. The performance improvement, especially the disproportionately large gains observed in the most sophisticated multi-hop and temporal reasoning tasks, implies that the hierarchical organizational quality and dynamic evolutionary capability of the context, rather than its mere length, are the key driving factors to remarkably boost the performance.

4.4. Parameter Sensitivity (Answering RQ3)

Figure 3 presents the sensitivity analysis of RGMem’s core parameters. For the context retrieval parameters (Figures 3(a)-3(c)), the results indicate that the model’s performance exhibits a robust, high-performance operating range around the selected default values, with performance degrading when the amount of retrieved contextual information is either insufficient or excessive. The analysis of the dynamic evolution threshold, θi​n​f\theta_{inf}(θs​u​m\theta_{sum}=2OPENθi​n​f)\theta_{inf}) (Figure 3(d)), provides empirical validation for the dynamic evolution mechanism itself: when the threshold is set too high (θi​n​f≥4\theta_{inf}\geq 4), performance drops sharply as necessary profile updates are suppressed, simulating a failure mode of a near-static model. Conversely, when the threshold is set too low (θi​n​f=2\theta_{inf}=2), performance also degrades due to over-sensitivity to noise. Performance peaks at the default value of θi​n​f=3\theta_{inf}=3, indicating that RGMem’s effectiveness stems from its ability to strike a critical balance between stability (avoiding noise) and plasticity (responding to changes).

5. Conclusion

In this paper, we propose a self-evolving memory framework RGMem inspired by the first principles of classic Renormalization Group in physics. We formalize, for the first time, the construction of conversational user profiles as a dynamical problem of variationally minimizing an Effective Hamiltonian Function across multiple scales. Our RGMem instantiates a series of renormalization transformation operators that drive the stable emergence of the user-profiling effective theory from high-noise microscopic evidence towards low-energy, highly-abstract macroscopic fixed points, and explains the profile’s non-linear phase transitions under paradigm-level impacts. To sum up, our framework provides a theoretical tool to investigate whether universality laws exist behind the evolution of different types of user profiles. This is not only about building better memories for machines, but also about profoundly understanding the intrinsic laws of human self-concept evolution. Therefore, we believe our work shed lights on understanding memory evolution, exploring interpretability, and even for revealing deeper mathematical structures underlying memory evolution in near future.

Appendix A More Details About Experiments

A.1. Dataset and Metrics

For a direct performance comparison with existing advanced memory systems, we conduct our experiments on the popular Long-term Conversational Memory (LOCOMO) (Maharana et al., 2024) benchmark, which is designed to evaluate the memory and reasoning capabilities of language models/agents over ultra-long conversation histories.

The dataset consists of 10 independent long-term conversations. On average, each conversation contains approximately 600 interaction turns and 26,000 tokens, accompanied by about 200 question-answer pairs. The evaluation paradigm involves providing the system with complete conversation history at first to build its memory or user profiling, after which the system is required to answer a series of questions regarding that conversation history. This evaluation paradigm enables to effectively test a system’s ability to construct and utilize long-term information.

The evaluation questions in LOCOMO are classified into four core categories to assess different dimensions of performance:

  • •

    Single-Hop Reasoning (S-Hop): This category of reasoning requires direct fact retrieval from a single piece of historical information.

  • •

    Multi-Hop Reasoning (M-Hop): This category of reasoning requires integrating and reasoning over multiple, non-contiguous pieces of historical information.

  • •

    Temporal Reasoning (Temp): This category of reasoning requires the understanding and tracking how information changes over time.

  • •

    Open-Domain (open): This category of reasoning involves broader knowledge.

A.2. Baseline Methods

To ensure a fair comparison with prior baseline works, we adhere to the established experimental setup in and exclude the "adversarial" category, which is designed to test the model’s ability to identify unanswerable questions. Furthermore, following prior works, we also adopt LLM-judge score as the primary metric and report performance across all four dimensions, as well as the Overall score, wherein GPT-4.1 is employed as the judge.

  • •

    Theoretical Upper Bound Method:
    Full-Context: This method provides the entire, unfiltered dialogue history to the LLM. It does not represent a practical system but serves as a crucial reference for the theoretical maximum of information availability.

  • •

    Standard Retrieval-Augmented Method:
    RAG-500: A standard RAG implementation that splits the dialogue history into 500-token chunks for dense vector retrieval. This baseline represents the prevailing flat memory paradigm based on a "chunk-and-retrieve" approach and serves to quantify the performance of a foundational RAG system.

  • •

    Memory-Augmented Methods:
    LangMem:     LangChain’s long-term memory module, which extracts and stores salient facts from conversations for later retrieval.
    Zep (Rasmussen et al., 2025): A prominent memory solution that constructs a temporal knowledge graph over user conversations, designed for fast semantic querying.
    Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025): An influential open-source memory system that incrementally compresses and stores memory facts using LLM-based summarization.
    Memobase: A profile-based memory module specifically designed to track persistent user attributes and preferences. As its goal is to explicitly model the user profiling, it serves as a direct and highly-relevant comparison with our work.

A.3. Implementation Details and Parameter Setting

All the experiments are based on gpt-4.1-mini as the language model/agent. In the implementation, the final context provided to the LLM is constructed via a multi-scale retrieval strategy that retrieves 5 core facts (λf​a​c​t\lambda_{fact}), 30 user conclusions (Λc​o​n​c\Lambda_{conc}) (using the BM25 algorithm for keyword retrieval), and 3 of the most relevant entities (filtered with a cosine similarity threshold of 0.5). The framework’s internal memory evolution dynamics are governed by the trigger thresholds of two core operators: the threshold θi​n​f\theta_{inf} for the relation inference operator (ℛK​1\mathcal{R}_{K1}) is set to 3, while the threshold θs​u​m\theta_{sum} for the community summarization operator (ℛK​2\mathcal{R}_{K2}) is set to 6. The hierarchical summarization operator (ℛK​2\mathcal{R}_{K2}) is manually triggered once after all dialogues have been processed to simulate periodic behavior.
